article_title: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market
citation: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Offer flexible pricing and licensing models — seat transfer, concurrent use, and pay-by-usage — because the adult learner population is constantly in flux
description: The guide recommends that entrepreneurs adopt hassle-free, flexible purchasing and licensing models as a core value proposition for learning providers. Because the adult learner market is constantly in flux, providers look for arrangements allowing reuse and transfer of seats among students, concurrent-use software, or pay-by-usage, especially during low enrollment. Flexibility should also extend to how and where tools are used, with learners able to access tools from their own devices wherever they are. The guide also advises offering group discounts to consortia and bundling professional development and ongoing support, citing a Digital Promise report that training and support is key to successful technology implementations.
requirements: Every tool should be designed to be easy to use without training, with professional development and ongoing support provided alongside it
constraints: The guide states entrepreneurs in education face a lengthy sales cycle even in adult learning, so licensing clarity and affordability matter
target_learners: adult learning providers such as community colleges, K-12 districts, libraries, and correctional institutions
target_learning_goals: expanding access to adult basic education and job-skills technology under constrained budgets
examples: The guide's Getting Started section instructs entrepreneurs to create hassle-free purchasing models that allow seat transfer and pay-by-usage where enrollment might be low
key_sources: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/36eceee2-6442-4c5c-8fa1-7b9e7eab4533

article_title: Integrating Digital Tools for Adult Learners: Four Critical Factors
citation: Constantakis, P. (2016). Integrating Digital Tools for Adult Learners: Four Critical Factors. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Support multiple, evolving blended implementation models with flexibility combined with structure
description: When integrating technology in adult education, administrators should set overall implementation requirements and goals while giving instructors autonomy over implementation details and allowing models to evolve as the learner population changes. The report states "Allowing for varied blended learning models like we found in this study is key with adult learners, even within one program, as there is no one way to meet the differing needs and levels of these learners."
requirements: Set overall implementation requirements and goals, such as number of hours spent
Give instructors autonomy for implementation details
Allow for and encourage evolving models
constraints: Most programs face a fairly transient population of adult learners, so the makeup of a course changes and technology use may need to change with it
target_learners: low-skilled adult learners in adult basic education programs
target_learning_goals: job-related skills through personalized digital learning
examples: Several study sites originally planned direct-instruction classroom models and adapted to allow learning lab or home use so learners needing more time with the product could get it
key_sources: Constantakis, P. (2016). Integrating Digital Tools for Adult Learners: Four Critical Factors. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/52ffa633-226c-445f-8113-54cc83dc76c7

article_title: Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention
citation: Wei Dai, Jionghao Lin, Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Yi-Shan Tsai, Namrata Srivastava, Pierre Le Bodic, Dragan Gašević, and Guanliang Chen. (2025). Learning Analytics for Early Identification of At-Risk Students and Feedback Intervention. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 102–125. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8735
title: Give students flexible options regarding whether and when to receive analytics-informed feedback support
description: This principle addresses intervention frequency and student control. Because preferences for intervention frequency vary, the article recommends that "students should be given flexible options regarding whether and when to receive this support." It follows from the survey finding that 60% of respondents wanted the intervention more often than the twice-per-semester schedule used, while others did not; the study's emails accordingly told students they could ask the teaching team not to receive the feedback again.
requirements: A delivery mechanism (e.g., email integrated with the LMS) that can support variable frequency and opt-out.
A way for students to communicate their preferences to the teaching team.
constraints: The study itself implemented only a fixed twice-per-semester frequency, so flexible scheduling was recommended, not tested.
target_learners: Undergraduate students identified as at risk of failing a course
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement with feedback interventions across the semester
examples: The intervention emails included the sentence: If you do not wish to receive this feedback again, please let the teaching team know directly.

article_title: FLIGHT (Facilitating Long-term Improvements in Graduation and Higher Education for Tomorrow)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2019). Transition to College intervention report: Facilitating Long-Term Improvements in Graduation and Higher Education for Tomorrow (FLIGHT)/Take Stock in Children (TSIC)®. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: FLIGHT's five-component support model combining scholarships, mentoring, case management, workshops, and student detail reports
description: FLIGHT organizes its services around five components: "The intervention included five components aimed at increasing the likelihood of students applying for, being accepted to, and enrolling in college." These are a pre-paid college scholarship for students who remain in good academic standing, one-on-one mentoring from adult volunteers, intensive case-management services from school staff, academic and college preparation workshops for students and their parents, and a year-end Student Detail Report of grades, attendance, test scores, and intervention status provided to parents, teachers, and guidance counselors. The model extends the TSIC® base with more intensive academic, attendance, and behavioral monitoring and added workshops.
requirements: Trained adult volunteer mentors meeting students a minimum of 15 sessions per year for at least 30 minutes; an assigned student advocate case manager; dedicated school-day space for meetings and workshops.
constraints: Cost information for FLIGHT was not reported in the reviewed study or on the TSIC® website; the WWC could only identify preliminary cost components.
target_learners: eligible low-income middle and high school students in grades 6 through the first three semesters of college
target_learning_goals: academic success and graduation on track
examples: Students in grades 7-10 participate in three workshops per year and students in grades 11-12 participate in six workshops per year, each lasting one to four hours; College Access and Success Meetings review progress toward graduation and college enrollment one to four times per year.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2019). article_title: Pivoting an In-Person Multiplatform Science Program to a Virtual Program during a Pandemic: Lessons Learned
citation: Li, L., Hayakawa, M., Freese, J., Daniels, B., Weiser, G., Luttgen, K., Lor, M. C., Schneider, M., Huang, C.-W., & Jensen, E. (2022). Pivoting an in-person transmedia science program to a virtual program during a pandemic: Lessons learned. Children, Youth and Environments, 32(3), 53-81. http://www.jstor.org/action/showPublication?journalCode=chilyoutenvi
title: Design multiplatform science programs for flexible implementation so educators can adapt delivery to their learning community
description: The article presents flexibility as a core design feature that enabled Hero Elementary's pivot to virtual delivery across formal and informal settings. "Educators are encouraged to customize Hero Elementary to suit their learning community by selecting high-interest playlists that align with their community’s goals, rather than presenting the materials in a specific, predetermined sequence." The developers reinforced this by providing distance-implementation documents, home versions of activities, and a train-the-trainer professional development model that "highlighted flexibility and adaptation," letting each site fit the program to its schedules, resources, and communities.
requirements: Modified resources must be presented to educators as learning materials that can be modified to accommodate a broad range of students, with supports such as Distance Implementation overview documents, Live Demo documents, Home Co-viewing Guides, and Discussion Guides.
constraints: The article stresses that each implementation was unique and all sites struggled with technology issues, whether unreliable internet connectivity or lack of technology support; flexibility does not remove access barriers.
target_learners: Kindergarten through second-grade students in formal and informal learning environments
Educators in formal classrooms and informal summer or after-school programs
target_learning_goals: Maintaining science learning access and engagement during abrupt transitions to virtual instruction
examples: Informal educators logged onto Zoom at scheduled times, shared screens on hands-on activities or animated episodes, reserved other activities for asynchronous use with debriefs, and used the advance and pause features of recorded videos to discuss activities with home materials.

article_title: Local Partnerships, National Impact: Year 1 of the Youth Mental Health Corps
citation: WestEd. (2025). Local Partnerships, National Impact: Year 1 of the Youth Mental Health Corps. https://www.wested.org/resource/building-a-model-of-student-centered-support-through-the-youth-mental-health-corps/
title: Adapt national youth-support programs through a flexible framework tailored to local contexts while maintaining core principles
description: The YMHC deliberately avoids a one-size-fits-all design: states design their own pathways aligned with local requirements and needs, while the national program maintains core principles. As the report states, "the program provides a flexible framework that can be tailored to local contexts while maintaining core principles of providing relationship-centered support and supporting workforce development." Partnering with local organizations builds buy-in and sustainability.
requirements: Local partners who understand their students' needs and existing support systems
Maintenance of core principles (relationship-centered support, workforce development) across adaptations
constraints: The report notes adaptability was demonstrated across four state contexts in Year 1; broader generalization is projected, not yet evaluated
target_learners: middle and high school students in urban, rural, and healthcare settings
examples: Colorado pairs members with sites via an intentional matching process; Minnesota rotates members across multiple rural sites; Texas delivers services in after-school hours

article_title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost
citation: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688
title: Keep organizational objectives flexible enough to incorporate AI-augmented work modes
description: The paper argues that whether AI adoption shows measured productivity gains depends on whether organizational performance indicators correspond to outputs AI can augment. It states: "The productivity impact of AI is maximized when organizational objectives are flexible enough to incorporate AI-augmented work modes, when evaluation criteria appropriately recognize AI-assisted contribution as individuals' own, and when goal-setting processes can adapt as AI capabilities evolve." Rigid objectives are modeled as an effective automation threshold below the technical first-best.
requirements: Evaluation criteria that recognize AI-assisted contribution as individuals' own
Goal-setting processes that can adapt as AI capabilities evolve
constraints: In domains where current AI is weak, such as manufacturing, flexible objectives alone cannot produce gains because AI does not influence the overall organizational goal
target_learning_goals: aligning performance evaluation with AI-augmented work modes
examples: The paper contrasts software engineering, where AI is already human-level capable and expected performance is stretched, with manufacturing where AI is weak

article_title: Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education
citation: Tseng, T., Seoror, L.H., Adda, J., Factor, M., Darabi, R., Matschke, K.R., Fu, T., Lin, A., Maram, A., Sinha, A. (2026). Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06721
title: Flowcode: an AI-powered creative coding environment integrating a code-structure flowchart with pedagogically constrained LLM explanations
description: Flowcode is a Node-based web application using GPT-4o that supports beginners iterating on found creative coding projects (Anime.js animations using HTML, CSS, and JS). Its interface has four components: code editors, a live preview, an LLM-generated flowchart summarizing project features across two abstraction levels, and an explanation panel producing "fill-in-the-blank code snippets" rather than full solutions. The system was refined across a pilot workshop and a lab study.
requirements: Requires an underlying LLM (GPT-4o) to generate flowchart JSON and beginner-oriented explanations
Designed for learners new to creative coding working on web-based animation projects
constraints: Evaluated only with a single model (GPT-4o), which the authors note may not represent other LLMs' performance
Studied over short 40-minute iteration periods; longer-term use unexplored
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students new to programming with web animation libraries
target_learning_goals: understanding existing code across HTML, CSS, and JS
iterating on found creative coding projects by actively writing code
examples: In the lab study, participants picked from four CodePen animation projects and iterated on them for 40 minutes while thinking aloud

article_title: Integrating Flipped Learning and Generative AI for Practice-Based Design Education: Evidence from a Knit Yarn Design Course
citation: Hong Qu, Zichao Ling, Yadie Yang. (2026). Integrating Flipped Learning and Generative AI for Practice-Based Design Education: Evidence from a Knit Yarn Design Course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18505
title: Integrated framework assigning complementary roles to flipped preparation, exemplar calibration, GenAI exploration, and studio refinement
description: The article proposes a pedagogical framework that connects flipped preparation, exemplar reference, GenAI-assisted visual exploration, and studio-based refinement in a practice-based design course. Rather than treating flipped learning and GenAI as separate innovations, the design "assigned them complementary roles: preparing, calibrating, exploring, making, and refining". Pre-class videos and readiness checks support preparation, the gallery provides feasible examples, the GenAI module supports early visual exploration, and instructor feedback with hands-on studio practice supports feasibility judgement and material realization. The authors state the framework helps explain why outcome differences appeared most clearly in creativity, design skills, and problem solving.
requirements: Pre-class activities must be structured and connected to in-class work rather than optional content delivery
GenAI-supported visual prototyping must be connected to clear criteria, reflective comparison, and subsequent physical making
constraints: GenAI outputs cannot reliably represent executable knitting instructions or physically feasible textile outcomes
Empirical support is from one small historical-cohort course implementation
target_learning_goals: knit yarn design combining visual ideation, material experimentation, and technical development
examples: The course used four lecture sessions and nine studio sessions, with pre-class micro-videos, embedded readiness checks, a curated gallery of thirteen yarn-type categories, and a parameter-guided GenAI ideation module
key_sources: Hong Qu, Zichao Ling, Yadie Yang. (2026). Integrating Flipped Learning and Generative AI for Practice-Based Design Education: Evidence from a Knit Yarn Design Course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18505

article_title: Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation
citation: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176
title: FlowComposer and the Continuator: interactive AI composition assistants
description: Two landmark composition assistants developed by François Pachet and collaborators at Sony CSL-Paris. FlowComposer is a score-centered assistant within the ERC Flow Machines project in which the musician can interactively write and edit a score and solicit melodic or harmonic sketches from a chosen stylistic corpus, with constraints imposed on generation. The Continuator operates at performance time, learning the style of a player from what they have just played and immediately continuing in that style, supporting real-time improvisation. Experiments with professional musicians and with children showed strong engagement, surprise, and a heightened sense of musical agency.
requirements: The composer must retain full intentionality and control over the compositional refinement process and structural and aesthetic decisions
constraints: Both systems are based on Markov models rather than current deep learning models, which the article notes are lighter and easier to integrate with constraints
examples: FlowComposer was used in creating the album Hello World in 2018; the Continuator generated strong engagement and heightened musical agency in experiments with professional musicians and children
key_sources: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176

article_title: Investigating the higher education institutions’ guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration
citation: Yunjo An, Ji Hyun Yu and Shadarra James. (2025). Investigating the higher education institutions' guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00507-3
title: Institutions should adopt flexible, stakeholder-specific GenAI policies addressing both opportunities and challenges
description: The article concludes that GenAI guidelines in higher education are rapidly evolving and that institutions need "flexible, stakeholder-specific policies that address both the opportunities and challenges presented by this technology". Its analysis shows guidelines vary widely by audience — 94% of universities had faculty guidelines but only 18% had researcher guidelines and 14% staff/administrator guidelines — supporting tailoring policies to each stakeholder group rather than issuing one generic policy.
requirements: Policies must be regularly updated as GenAI tools and guidelines constantly evolve; clear roles and responsibilities among faculty, students, and administrators are needed
constraints: The article notes many existing AI guidelines are generic and do not specifically address issues caused by GenAI in higher education
target_learners: higher education administrators, faculty, students, researchers, and staff
examples: The study analyzed guidelines for five audiences separately and found faculty guidelines covered seven themes while staff/administrator guidelines covered three, all seven staff-targeted guidelines addressing privacy and data protection

Investigating the higher education institutions' guidelines and policies regarding the use of generative AI in teaching, learning, research, and administration. article_title: Cognitive benefits of last night's sleep: daily variations in children's sleep behavior are related to working memory fluctuations
citation: Könen, T., Dirk, J., & Schmiedek, F. (2015). Cognitive benefits of last night's sleep: daily variations in children's sleep behavior are related to working memory fluctuations. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 56(2), 171–182. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.12296
title: FLUX smartphone ambulatory assessment application for children's daily sleep and working memory measurement
description: A dedicated smartphone application developed by the Technology Based Assessment Group at the DIPF for the FLUX project ('Assessment of Cognitive Performance FLUctuations in the School ConteXt'). It was the only available function of the distributed Dell Streak 5 phones, with internet, calls, games, and the regular system menu blocked, and delivered numerical and spatial working memory updating tasks plus sleep and tiredness items at three fixed daily occasions in school and at home for 31 consecutive days.
requirements: Fixed timing in school so teachers could schedule instruction, supervised sessions by teachers and trained research assistants, and individually adapted timing windows out of school
constraints: The application was pretested with 12 third-graders on 15 occasions and the tasks and items were pretested with 75 elementary school children before the main study
target_learning_goals: measuring daily working memory updating performance and self-reported sleep behavior in children's everyday lives
examples: Children completed numerical and spatial working memory updating tasks embedded in a child-appropriate story, with four blocks per occasion yielding 40 responses, and could press a 'no idea' button to refuse self-report items

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Represent telemetry data in a format requiring minimal preprocessing, such as a flat file, for non-programmer end users
description: Assuming a typical research environment where programmers may be unavailable, the chapter recommends ease of use over computational efficiency: "We recommend a ﬂat ﬁle representation of the data as this format is simple, easy to explain, easily understood, and portable." More expressive formats like JSON or SQL require a database connection and programming skill, whereas the data's destination is a statistical analysis tool used mostly by non-programmers. A sample flat-file format with fields such as time stamp, user_id, data_code, and game_state is provided.
requirements: A predefined record format so data flow directly into statistical analysis tools
An assumption of multiple data analysts and researchers touching the data over its life span
constraints: The guideline may not apply in high volume environments with dedicated programmers and storage constraints
target_learners: researchers and data analysts without programming experience
target_learning_goals: analyzing game telemetry to derive measures of learning and performance
examples: Table 3.1 shows a flat-file telemetry format with a serial number, time stamp, game_time, user_id, stage, level, data_code, data_description, value fields, and game_state

article_title: Integrating Culture in the Design of ICTs
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2008). Integrating Culture in the Design of ICTs. British Journal of Educational Technology, Vol 39 No 1, 6-17. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00699.x
title: Fleer's design principles for culturally specific educational software
description: The article reports a set of design principles derived from cultural research on Australian Aborigines and used to guide software development specific to that audience. The principles focused on 'making the content familiar; including familiar graphics and text; replicating family life and ideologies; supporting academic strengths; incorporating learning strategies; engaging learner-controlled learning; and a ﬂexible design'. The example is described as more specialised than generic, grounding software in the target audience's cultural experiences and ideologies.
requirements: Cultural research describing the target audience's learning strategies and contexts for learning should ground the principles
constraints: The article characterises this example as more specialised than generic on the culture based circumference
target_learners: Australian Aboriginal learners, as reported in the cited Fleer (1989) review
target_learning_goals: Software that accurately represents Aboriginal abilities, knowledge and ideologies and prepares learners for the dominant culture
examples: Fleer used her review of empirical research as a guide in developing design principles that guided development of software specific to teaching Australian Aborigines

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Cognitive flexibility arises from interplay of nodes within the executive control network rather than a distinct substrate
description: The authors propose that "Cognitive flexibility likely emerges from the interplay of specific nodes in the frontal and parietal cortices" which are not flexibility-specific but are activated across executive functions. Within the domain-general executive control network, "the specific computations among nodes and their anatomical specificity within the broader frontoparietal networks determine which EF is behaviorally observed." Temporal dynamics of inter-node connectivity may distinguish executive functions; salience, dorsal and ventral attention networks, vlPFC and IFJ are proposed to act in sequence during a switch.
requirements: Working memory load must be controlled in task designs to avoid confounds
Causal modeling studies are needed for validation
constraints: The model is speculative at this time and remains to be validated with future causal modeling studies
target_learning_goals: understanding neural mechanisms of flexible cognition
key_sources: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003

article_title: Association and dissociation between judgments of learning and memory: A Meta-analysis of the font size effect
citation: Chang, M., Brainerd, C.J. (2022). Association and dissociation between judgments of learning and memory: A Meta-analysis of the font size effect. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09287-3
title: Fluency-based account: font size memory effects are tied to (dis)fluency but JOL effects are not
description: The article's working explanation separates the two font size effects mechanistically. Memory effects of font size are attributed to perceptual (dis)fluency, whereas JOL effects arise through other bases (e.g., beliefs), so the two can diverge in some font-size ranges. The authors state: "Our working explanation is that the memory effects of font size are tied to (dis)fluency, but its JOL effects are not." This account organizes the meta-analytic moderator pattern, including the restricted range of dissociation.
requirements: A range of font sizes spanning fluent and disfluent categories so that fluency-based memory effects and non-fluency-based JOL effects can be distinguished
constraints: The article labels this a working explanation, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: Adult learners in laboratory memory experiments studying word lists
target_learning_goals: Calibration of self-monitoring judgments (JOLs) with actual memory performance
examples: The meta-analysis classified font sizes against a 17–161 pt. fluent range established with a fixed 85 cm viewing distance, and found the quadratic font size–fluency relation remained robust when viewing distance was not fixed
key_sources: Chang, M., Brainerd, C.J. (2022). Association and dissociation between judgments of learning and memory: A Meta-analysis of the font size effect. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09287-3

article_title: Foreign Language Attainment of Children/Adolescents with Poor Literacy Skills: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: von Hagen, A., Kohnen, S., & Stadie, N. (2021). Foreign Language Attainment of Children/Adolescents with Poor Literacy Skills: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09566-6
title: Evidence corpus of 16 studies (968 participants) on foreign language attainment in poor readers/spellers, with datasets and code on the Open Science Framework
description: The review assembled a corpus of 16 group-comparison studies with 968 participants (404 poor readers/spellers, 564 controls), all assessing English as a foreign language, identified via a PRISMA-guided search across Ovid databases, PubMed, ProQuest, Web of Science and gray-literature sources. The authors state that "the datasets and code used to compute the analyses can be accessed on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/np97f/". The corpus supported meta-analyses on 10 of 15 foreign language outcome measures.
requirements: Studies must compare poor readers/spellers with control participants with typical literacy skills on a foreign language outcome measure, with literacy status confirmed by test rather than self- or teacher report
constraints: Only studies of English as a foreign language were available
Participants had little or no access to the foreign language outside classroom instruction
target_learners: children and adolescents in primary and secondary education with poor literacy skills
target_learning_goals: foreign language attainment subskills such as phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, and reading comprehension
examples: Round 1 of the search screened 1370 references after duplicate removal and ended with 16 included studies; a second round of reference checking added none

article_title: Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement
citation: Prast, E. J., Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Van Luit, J. E. H. (2018). Differentiated instruction in primary mathematics: Effects of teacher professional development on student achievement. Learning and Instruction, 54, 22-34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.009
title: Use flexible within-class ability grouping coupled with instructional adaptation to protect low-achieving students from negative grouping effects
description: The article argues that negative effects of ability grouping for low-achieving students, ascribed to stigmatization and lower educational quality in low-ability groups, can be prevented. Negative stigma may be overcome by ensuring subgroups are within-class and flexible and by promoting a growth mindset, communicating additional instruction as an opportunity to learn rather than a sign of fixed low ability. When grouping is used to adapt education to the specific needs of students in the groups, it may enhance rather than reduce educational quality for low achievers because instruction is better attuned to their needs.
requirements: Subgroups must be within-class and flexible
Participation in additional instruction should be communicated as an opportunity to learn, not as a sign of fixed low ability
Instruction and practice must actually be adapted to the educational needs of the different ability groups
constraints: Reviews found slight negative effects of within-class ability grouping in primary school across three studies in which variations in instructional treatment were not explicitly described
target_learners: Primary school students of low, average and high achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement growth for all achievement groups, including low-achieving students
examples: The GROW study used flexible within-class achievement groups (typically low-, average-, and high-achieving) that students could switch between based on changes in educational needs

Learning and Instruction, 54, 22-34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.009

article_title: Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations
citation: Laura Gabler, Stefan Ufer. (2024). Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101902
title: Flexibility in dealing with additive situations: restructuring situation models via the Inversion and Dynamization strategies
description: The article defines "flexibility in dealing with additive situations as the skill to restructure situation models of additive one-step word problems by inferring additional features of the situation structure (a/s wording, semantic structure, unknown set)". It is operationalized through two strategies: the Inversion Strategy, which reverses subject and object and inverts additive/subtractive wording to turn inconsistent problems into consistent ones, and the Dynamization Strategy, which restructures static compare problems as dynamic equalize problems. The framework builds on Kintsch's text comprehension model and Riley et al.'s problem-type taxonomy, and holds that inferring additional situation-structure features can ease identifying an adequate mathematical model even with restricted conceptual knowledge.
requirements: Learners need conceptual knowledge about how features of a situation structure relate to mathematical concepts, and the relevant schemata must be individually available and activated
constraints: The framework addresses additive one-step word problems without irrelevant information; equalize problems have little evidence on difficulty since they were not included in the majority of studies
target_learning_goals: flexibly restructuring situation models of additive situations
examples: The flexibility test contrasted statement pairs equivalent via the Dynamization Strategy (contrasting semantic structures) or the Inversion Strategy (contrasting a/s wordings), embedded in a story about twins reporting on a birthday party
key_sources: Laura Gabler, Stefan Ufer. (2024). Training flexibility in dealing with additive situations. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101902

article_title: A change of scenery: Does the setting of an instructional video affect learning?
citation: Merkt, M., Lux, S., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Schwan, S. (2020). A Change of Scenery: Does the Setting of an Instructional Video Affect Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000414
title: Setting-manipulated instructional videos on floral diagrams and floral formulas (greenhouse vs. white wall)
description: Two versions of an instructional video about floral diagrams and floral formulas were produced, differing only in setting: one was "shot in a greenhouse (authentic setting)" and one "in front of a white wall (neutral setting)". Experiment 1 used these videos to test whether the setting affects retention and application of the content, and the same learning materials were used again in Experiment 2.
requirements: Content is held constant across versions so that the setting is the differing factor between the authentic and neutral videos.
constraints: The retention benefit observed with these materials in Experiment 1 did not replicate in Experiment 2 despite the same learning materials and a comparable sample.
target_learners: adult participants watching instructional videos in laboratory experiments

article_title: Fluctuations in elementary school children’s working memory performance in the school context.
citation: Dirk, Judith; Schmiedek, Florian. (2016). Fluctuations in elementary school children's working memory performance in the school context. The journal of educational psychology 108 (2016) 5, S. 722-739. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000076
title: Performance fluctuations across and within days as a consideration for theories of cognitive development and learning
description: The article proposes that accounts of cognitive development and learning should incorporate short-timescale performance variability. It argues that "Theories about cognitive development and learning should consider performance fluctuations across and within days to understand the processes underlying long-term changes." The proposal is grounded in the finding that day-to-day, occasion-to-occasion, and moment-to-moment variability each contribute roughly equally to observed daily WM fluctuations, with large individual differences.
requirements: Theories must model within-person variability at multiple timescales, not only long-term average performance
constraints: The article presents this as a foundation for future research on antecedents and consequences of fluctuating cognitive resources, not as a tested theory
target_learners: elementary school children (8 to 11 years old)
target_learning_goals: understanding processes underlying long-term cognitive development and learning
examples: The ambulatory assessment study decomposed daily WM variability into day-to-day, occasion-to-occasion, and moment-to-moment components

article_title: Education shapes the structure of semantic memory and impacts creative thinking
citation: Denervaud, S., Christensen, A. P., Kenett, Y. N. & Beaty, R. E. (2021). Education shapes the structure of semantic memory and impacts creative thinking. npj Science of Learning 6:35. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00113-8
title: Cognitive network science framework of flexible semantic memory structure
description: The article applies a cognitive network science framework in which semantic memory is represented as a network of concept nodes and similarity edges, characterized by clustering coefficient (CC), average shortest path length (ASPL), and modularity (Q). A "flexible" structure has "high connectivity (higher CC, lower Q) and short path lengths between concepts (lower ASPL)" and is thought to support creative thinking by keeping remotely associated concepts closer. The study uses this framework to test whether educational experience shapes children's knowledge representation.
requirements: Verbal fluency data processed into binary response matrices with identical node sets across groups (TMFG filtering retains 3n–6 edges) so network measures are comparable.
constraints: Modularity in semantic networks is stated to be inversely related to a network's flexibility; the framework's application here is group-based and could not link individual network metrics to creativity scores.
target_learning_goals: concept learning and knowledge representation in semantic memory
examples: The study estimated semantic networks from 60-second animal-category verbal fluency data of Montessori and traditionally schooled children and compared CC, ASPL and Q between groups.

article_title: Introduction to IJAIED Special Issue, FATE in AIED
citation: Beverly Woolf, Kaska Porayska-Pomsta, Wayne Holmes, Ken Holstein. (2022). Introduction to IJAIED Special Issue, FATE in AIED. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00299-x
title: A sufficient ethics framework for AIED must be flexible and draw on the learning sciences and related fields
description: This is the editorial's normative account of what an ethics framework for AI in education requires. It argues that "any sufficient framework for ethics of AIED needs to include insights from the learning sciences, cognitive and educational neuroscience" and from fields whose impact has not yet been felt in education technology. The framework must also support flexibility to incorporate new knowledge as science, socio-cultural norms, values and educational systems emerge and adapt, because AIED is a design discipline, not solely an empirical science. The editorial presents this as an argued position, not a tested result.
requirements: Must include insights from the learning sciences, cognitive and educational neuroscience, and other fields not yet felt in education technology
constraints: The editorial states designing such a framework is challenging, requires many years of focus, and must accommodate unknown unknowns as well as known unknowns
target_learners: AIED researchers and practitioners designing AI-based educational technologies
target_learning_goals: Ethical design, development and deployment of AI-supported instructional systems

citation: Tom Murray. (2003). MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.199-233. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197317
title: Provide flexible, adaptive on-line learning material to support opportunistic active reading
description: The article recommends providing textbook-like content in a flexible manner that supports "opportunistic processes of active reading and learning". Through adaptive methods, one online artifact can serve learners with diverse goals and backgrounds, and the material is designed to support inquiry, exploratory, and curiosity-driven learning in richly interconnected content.
requirements: Adaptive methods so a single artifact can address diverse user goals and backgrounds
constraints: Usability issues arise in such open-ended learning environments and must be addressed deliberately
target_learners: learners with diverse goals and backgrounds
examples: MetaLinks hyperbooks provide textbook-like content in a flexible manner supporting opportunistic active reading.

article_title: Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Yizhou Fan, Wannisa Matcha, Nora’ayu Ahmad Uzir, Qiong Wang, Dragan Gašević. (2021). Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 980–1021. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00249-z
title: Flipped Classroom MOOC with diverse unit-level learning designs as research context
description: A seven-week MOOC developed by a Chinese university in 2014 and offered on the iCourse 163 platform, targeting in-service and pre-service teachers. Each unit followed a different design: "Unit 1 followed a traditional lecture-based design", Unit 2 case-based learning, Unit 3 project-based, Unit 4 case-based with reading activities, and Unit 5 problem-based. The article states that "it is precisely this variety and diversity of the learning design that made this MOOC unique and provided a suitable research context to address the research questions".
requirements: Each unit uses different learning resources and offers different learning pathways to cater to different pedagogical intentions
constraints: No unit quiz and peer review were offered for unit 0 and unit 6; the study used offerings from the 4th to the 16th round, after the curriculum structure stabilised
target_learners: in-service and pre-service teachers in China
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying the flipped classroom pedagogy in daily teaching practice
examples: Unit 2 asked learners to write their own teaching plan, graded through peer review; Unit 3 required learners to produce a teaching video

citation: Kinshuk, Chen, N.-S., Cheng, I.-L., & Chew, S. W. (2016). Evolution Is not enough: Revolutionizing Current Learning Environments to Smart Learning Environments. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0108-x
title: Flipped classroom as a student-centered blended learning environment in smart learning settings
description: The flipped classroom is presented as a popular method for enhancing teaching quality and improving learners' outcomes, particularly gaining interest in K-12 education (Chen et al. 2014). The paper states that "By integrating various learning technologies in the classroom, the flipped classroom approach has shifted the instruction from a teacher centered physical classroom, to a student centered blended learning environment." It enables interactive learning activities inside and outside the physical classroom and combines formal and informal learning approaches to increase student engagement.
requirements: Integration of various learning technologies in the classroom
target_learners: K-12 students (where the approach has gained particular interest)
target_learning_goals: increased student engagement and improved learning outcomes through student-centered blended learning
examples: Students take a vital role through collaborative activities while course content is delivered interactively both inside and outside class

article_title: Implementation of the flipped classroom and its longitudinal impact on improving academic performance
citation: Torres-Martín, C., Acal, C., El-Homrani, M., & Mingorance-Estrada, Á. C. (2022). Implementation of the flipped classroom and its longitudinal impact on improving academic performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10095-y
title: Flipped classroom implementation requires sustained access to a fully equipped technology classroom
description: The article's longitudinal data show that the flipped classroom methodology depends on reliable access to a "fully equipped classroom with technological resources". In the one academic year (2017/2018) when such a classroom was only occasionally available, a mixed methodology had to be used and average grades declined. The authors state this reinforces "the connection between the usual use of technological resources and the flipped classroom methodology".
requirements: A technology classroom with a computer for each student must be available for regular use during face-to-face sessions.
constraints: When a fully equipped technology classroom is unavailable, the methodology degrades into a mixed approach and the performance benefit is reduced.
target_learners: university students in a first-year education degree subject
examples: In 2017/2018, when "there was not a fully equipped classroom with technological resources", a mixed methodology was carried out and grades declined.

title: Prepare for student resistance and unequal technological readiness when introducing the flipped classroom
description: The article identifies three limitations when starting the flipped classroom: "resistance to change, technological aspects and teaching perspectives". Students accustomed to traditional methodology face a period of progressive familiarization, and "not all students have basic skills in the use of technological resources". The authors recommend a progressive adaptation period and inviting a former student to share their experience.
requirements: A process of progressive familiarization and successive adaptation, which can last the first month of the course.
constraints: Not all students have basic technological skills or the same resources at home, so previous teaching work must be adapted to available resources.
target_learners: university students accustomed to traditional teaching methodology
examples: The authors suggest inviting "a student from the previous course to explain the experience to the students of the new course".

article_title: Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education
citation: Lee, J., Lim, C., & Kim, H. (2017). Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9502-1
title: A design model for flipped learning in higher education that integrates online and face-to-face sessions
description: The article develops a prescriptive instructional design model for flipped learning (FL) that guides designers through analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation of both online and face-to-face components. The model treats online lectures and F2F activities as "core complementary constituents of the learning experience as a coherent whole" rather than as supplementary additions. It was validated through expert review, usability testing, and field evaluation.
requirements: Requires a design team or instructor able to create and curate online video lectures and facilitate interactive F2F sessions
constraints: Designed for higher education contexts; the authors note that FL design involves "considerable intricacy" and "practically infinite design variability in diverse contexts"

article_title: Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education
citation: Lee, J., Lim, C., & Kim, H. (2017). Development of an instructional design model for flipped learning in higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9502-1
title: Design online and face-to-face components as core complementary constituents rather than supplementary additions
description: The article argues that effective flipped learning requires treating online and face-to-face components as equally essential, not layering one on top of the other. It states that "neither component has a supplementary role, but rather each is a core complementary constituent of the learning experience as a coherent whole." This principle guides the allocation of content between modes in the model's analysis phase.
requirements: Requires analysis of which content is best suited to online delivery versus F2F interaction before design begins
constraints: The article notes that blending "does not mean simply combining the two or laying one on top of the other" and that typical mixes fail to achieve the benefits of either mode
examples: The model's analysis step allocates basic concepts to online portions and difficult materials requiring peer or teacher help to F2F sessions

title: Flipped learning course structure with online lectures before F2F collaborative problem-solving sessions
description: The article describes a recurring lesson structure in which students watch online lectures individually before class and then engage in group problem-solving activities during F2F sessions. In the field evaluation, students discussed problems in teams and then participated in whole-class discussion, with problem difficulty gradually increasing over class time.
requirements: Requires online content to be prerequisite for F2F activities, with a tight link between what students do in class and at home
examples: Students engaged in group problem-solving activities with three to four problems provided by the instructors, with difficulty gradually increasing

citation: Yan Shen, Dan Spencer, Jennifer Tagsold, Hyunsong Kim. (2025). Integrating cognition, self-regulation, motivation, and metacognition: a framework of post-pandemic flipped classroom design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10485-y
title: Flipped learning cycle design pattern: defined cycles with gradually increasing challenge and regular specific feedback across online, in-class, and after-class steps
description: A repeatable lesson-level pattern in which each flipped learning cycle encompasses online, in-class, and after-class learning steps. Cycles should be "as consistent in length and steps as possible", with tasks designed by selectively applying the First Principles of Instruction; challenge levels should gradually increase along the cycle, from introductory online tasks to less structured in-class whole problems to after-class problems at sustained or increased complexity with reduced support; and regular, specific intrinsic and corrective feedback should be provided throughout the cycle steps to sustain students' self-perception of competence.
requirements: Defining the FL cycle length based on a regular class schedule makes the FL cycles easier to plan
Individual assistance should be offered when the challenge levels are likely to be above any particular student's abilities
constraints: Although there are mixed findings about whether the reduction of class time affects learning outcomes, the decision should be made based on the benefits of reduced class size, the students' existing SRL skills, and the amount of SRL support available
examples: Spencer et al. (2022) created flipped learning cycles guiding students through online lessons and assessments, in-class small-group problem solving, and independent after-class problems

article_title: Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds
citation: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815
title: Floreo VR and Google Arts & Culture platforms used as the VR social competence education materials
description: The intervention combined two VR applications across eight sessions. Floreo VR "teaches children social, behavioral, communication, and life skills through a range of simulations concerning children's daily life scenarios", delivered via Cardboard VR with instructor guidance; the research team selected only inclusive-learning modules since some are designed for children with autism spectrum disorder. examples: Eight 25–45 min VR sessions with 3–5 lessons each; virtual scenarios in classroom, playground, canteen, and library settings

citation: Li, X., Li, T., Yan, L., Li, Y., Zhao, L., Raković, M., Molenaar, I., Gašević, D., & Fan, Y. (2025). FLoRA: An Advanced AI-Powered Engine to Facilitate Hybrid Human-AI Regulated Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07362
title: FLoRA Engine
description: The FLoRA Engine is an AI-powered learning platform that integrates generative AI and learning analytics to detect, measure, and facilitate self-regulated learning (SRL). It provides instrumentation tools such as collaborative writing, multi-agent chatbots, and detailed learning trace logging to support dynamic, adaptive scaffolding of self-regulation tailored to individual needs in real time. The engine is designed to support hybrid human-AI regulated learning (HHAIRL) by providing targeted, timely scaffolding while preserving learners' role as active decision-makers.
requirements: Integration with a learning management system (Moodle)

article_title: Does the Flipped Classroom Improve Student Learning and Satisfaction? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Torstein Låg, Rannveig Grøm Sæle. (2019). Does the Flipped Classroom Improve Student Learning and Satisfaction? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419870489
title: Working definition of the flipped classroom as moving teacher-centered instruction out of the classroom to free time for student-centered activities
description: The article proposes a deliberately theory-neutral definition: "The flipped classroom is a teaching model that moves most of the teacher-centered instruction out of the classroom to free up time in the classroom for more student-centered learning activities." Unlike definitions requiring social activities or mandatory pre/postclass tasks, it prescribes no particular pedagogy, aiming to describe the model's general effect rather than prescribe practice. Traditional teaching is defined as predominantly teacher-centered, lecture-based information transfer.
requirements: For inclusion in the meta-analysis, most information transfer had to be moved outside and prior to class, most in-session teaching had to involve active learning, and the control condition had to be predominantly teacher centered and lecture based
constraints: The theory-neutrality may lead to a lack of pedagogical rationale on which to design intervention specifics, leaving teachers and students to a trial-and-error approach, as the article notes citing Bishop and Verleger (2013) and Lundin et al. (2018)
target_learners: students at any level of education, primary through further education
target_learning_goals: academic achievement on exams, tests, and grades; pass rates; student satisfaction with teaching
examples: Studies were included only if published 2010 or later, when interventions were explicitly labeled as flipped classrooms

article_title: The Meta-Analysis of the Studies about the Effects of Flipped Learning on Students' Achievement
citation: Aydin, M., Okmen, B., Sahin, S., & Kilic, A. (2021). The Meta-Analysis of the Studies About the Effects of Flipped Learning on Students' Achievement. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 22(1), Article 3. https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: The F-L-I-P framework of flipped learning: flexible environment, learning culture, intentional content, professional educators
description: The article presents the Flipped Learning Network's 2014 framework of four basic components forming the acronym F-L-I-P: "1) Flexible environment, 2) Learning culture, 3) Intentional content, and 4) Professional educators". Flexible environments can be regulated by educators and students at will; the educator stops being the source of information and guides student-centered exploration; content is designed around learning objectives and points of difficulty; and educators continuously observe, give feedback, and evaluate students. The article uses this framework as the theoretical background for defining the flipped learning model whose achievement effects it meta-analyzes.
requirements: Lessons are transferred to students by means of videos outside of class, with in-class time spent on problem-solving and individual or group studies
Educators must observe students continuously, give feedback, and evaluate them
constraints: The framework is presented as background definition, not tested in this study's meta-analysis
target_learners: students at primary, secondary, high school, associate, and undergraduate levels
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in experimental and social science lessons
examples: The 25 meta-analyzed studies implemented flipped learning across science and social science lessons with pretest/posttest experimental control group designs

article_title: The Impact of Flipped Classroom on College Students' Academic Performance: A Meta-Analysis Based on 20 Experimental Studies
citation: Zhang, Q., Cheung, E.S.T., & Cheung, C.S.T. (2021). The impact of flipped classroom on college students’ academic performance: A meta-analysis based on 20 experimental studies. Science Insights Education Frontiers, 8(2):1059-1080. https://doi.org/10.15354/sief.21.re019
title: Flipped classroom as a blended learning model that moves knowledge transfer before class and internalization into class
description: The article defines the flipped classroom as a teaching model in which students study instructional videos or other electronic materials before class and use class time for cooperative, interactive learning and knowledge internalization. It describes it as "a brand-new, deep-level blended learning model" integrating traditional classroom teaching and online learning, reversing teacher and student roles from lecturer/passive to instructor/active. The meta-analysis evaluates this model's impact on college academic performance.
requirements: Knowledge transfer must be completed before class via learning resources so classroom time can be used to guide internalization
Students must be able to choose learning resources and self-pace according to their learning situation

title: Flipped learning as a social-constructivist, student-centred model grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
description: The article frames flipped learning as a constructivist-inspired approach in which learners build their own understanding through in-class collaborative activities, combining peer-assisted, collaborative and problem-based learning with technology-driven pre-class activities. It draws on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, "the distance between the actual developmental level as determined by independent problem solving" and the level reachable with adult guidance or capable peers, so pre-class content lets students learn fundamentals at home and internalise new tasks through interaction in class.
requirements: Pre-class preparation (videos or presentations) completed before face-to-face sessions
In-class collaborative activities with lecturer and peers
Instructor scaffolding and awareness of FL affordances
constraints: Not all students adjust easily or take an active role; some prefer traditional lecture and passive learning (Engin, 2014, as cited)
examples: The IET-112 course used recorded lecture videos with embedded quiz forms before class, and structured/unstructured discussion, circle of voices and fishbowl formations during class.

title: Flipped-course pattern: pre-class videos with monitored quiz forms, in-class group activities, and after-class group work
description: The article's experimental course followed a structured flipped pattern: before class, EG students watched 10-15 minute recorded lecture videos in staged steps and completed electronic forms with 3-5 random questions, which served to monitor activity and guide preparation; during class, the FL model was implemented "through group discussion and in-class activities" using varied group-work techniques; after class, students did group work and assignments. Electronic forms to monitor and structure pre-class viewing
Classroom arrangements (chair positioning, data show projection) appropriate for group activity
constraints: Videos longer than 10 minutes were perceived as time-consuming and slowed progress through the steps
examples: EG students completed five steps before class, including watching videos lasting 10-15 minutes and answering 3-5 random questions per video via a browser form shared by WhatsApp and email.

article_title: Foreign Language Learning in Primary School: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Meg Wiggins, Constanza Gonzalez Parrao, Helen Austerberry and Anne Ingold. (2017). Foreign Language Learning in Primary School: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Foreign Language Learning (FLL) curriculum: 18-week French programme with linked English literacy activities for Year 3 and 4
description: The FLL programme, created by the Education Development Trust, is a curriculum-based programme of weekly 45-minute French lessons with linked 15-30 minute English literacy follow-up activities, delivered to whole classes over three half-terms (18 weeks). Each half-term unit included six step-by-step French lesson plans covering "French vocabulary, grammar, and phonology within themed topic areas", with follow-up English activities focused on extending English vocabulary, phonology, and grammar/punctuation. requirements: Teachers were provided with detailed lesson plans and three days of training in delivering the curriculum
constraints: The curriculum was meant to be followed closely, but with allowance for adaptation by teachers who were confident in French language teaching
target_learners: Year 3 and Year 4 primary school pupils (age 7-9) in England
target_learning_goals: French as a foreign language (vocabulary, grammar, phonology)

citation: Marina Milovanoviü, Jasmina Obradoviü, Aleksandar Milajiü. (2013). APPLICATION OF INTERACTIVE MULTIMEDIA TOOLS IN TEACHING MATHEMATICS – EXAMPLES OF LESSONS FROM GEOMETRY. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Macromedia Flash multimedia lessons on isometric transformations and regular polyhedra
description: A set of interactive multimedia lessons created in Macromedia Flash 10.0 covering isometric transformations (line and point reflection, translation, rotation) and regular polyhedra. constraints: The post-test was solved without using the computers, so the element supports learning rather than test-taking

citation: Maryam Eslahcar Komachali, Mohammadreza Khodareza. (2012). The Effect of Using Vocabulary Flash Card on Iranian Pre-University Students' Vocabulary Knowledge. International Education Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n3p134
title: Use flash cards so learners can sort words by difficulty and practise retrieval
description: The article recommends flash cards over traditional presentation because they let learners manage their own review and retrieval. It states "new words can easily be practiced extensively with flash card. Learners can separate cards into several categories based on their difficulty level," which helps them review difficult words more frequently, and that presenting the L2 word with its definition on the other side lets learners practise recalling meanings. The article also argues traditional method causes rote learning and uneven attention to words.
requirements: Cards bearing the L2 word on one side and its definition or L1 translation on the other
constraints: The article's supporting evidence is its own single experimental study with female pre-university students
target_learners: EFL learners preparing for exams such as TOEFL and GRE, per the article's implications
target_learning_goals: vocabulary retention and retrieval of new words
examples: The article attributes the four stated reasons for flash card effectiveness to Mondria & Mondria-de Vries (1994), Nakata (2008), and Schmitt & Schmitt (1995)

article_title: The Impact of the Flipped Classroom Model on Students' Academic Achievement
citation: Emine Cabi. (2018). The Impact of the Flipped Classroom Model on Students' Academic Achievement. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 19(3). https://www.irrodl.org
title: The Flipped Classroom Model as a two-component pedagogical model with four implementation components
description: The article defines the FC Model as "a new pedagogical model where the instructor shares predetermined digital resources with students through a platform outside the classroom, and related content is also taught through this outside platform asynchronously". Citing Bishop and Verleger (2013), it identifies two significant components: computer technologies such as video lectures, and interactive learning activities. It further lists four components from the Flipped Learning Network (2014): flexible environment, learner-centered detailed content teaching, intentional monitoring of progress with active learning strategies, and a professional educator who provides immediate feedback. In this study the model was implemented with Khan Academy videos out of class and Kahoot quizzes plus group presentations in class.
requirements: Instructors share predetermined digital resources through an outside-of-class platform
In-class sessions carry active, collaborative, interactive problem-solving activities
The instructor monitors students, provides immediate feedback, and assesses outputs
constraints: The article notes students had difficulty adapting because it is a new approach, citing Chen Hsieh et al. (2017)
examples: Out-of-class Khan Academy videos on information theory topics; in-class Kahoot multiple-choice assessments and weekly group presentations with rotating roles

article_title: Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos
citation: Faisal M. Almutairi, Abdullah A. Almodaires & Alaa J. Zeyab. (2020). Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos. International Education Studies, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v13n7p163
title: Six-week flipped video-production workshop course at PAAET's College of Basic Education
description: The experimental setting was a six-week workshop course on generating digital videos at the Department of Educational Technology, PAAET's College of Basic Education in Kuwait, taught by the same instructor in two classrooms during the 2018-2019 summer semester. In the flipped condition, "the students in the experimental group were taught in a blended learning context where the flipped learning model was applied": demonstration videos and readings before class, hands-on collaborative activities in class, and homework after class. The control group received lectures and direct teaching with homework. Pre- and post-tests of ten multiple-choice items assessed technical video-production knowledge.
requirements: All learning materials, including videos, course content, pre-test and post-test quiz and feedback questionnaire, were released to the respective student groups
constraints: The course was a single video-production unit in one department at one Kuwaiti college, so findings were not interpreted beyond the sampled population
target_learners: pre-service teachers enrolled in technology integration courses at a teacher-training college
target_learning_goals: technical skills and knowledge for creating and editing digital videos
examples: The instructor used demonstration videos covering production scale, shooting style and techniques, camera movement and post-production editing; the experimental group worked through in-class activities guided by the instructor and peers

description: The researcher developed an instructional program in MacroMedia Flash Professional Version 6 to teach the passive voice to first-secondary pupils. It is organized into sections covering construction, use, agent, present, past and modal verbs in the passive, and problematic issues, each with "Explanation and Examples: presented in an audio-visual manner" plus exercises, drills, and a Test Yourself section. article_title: Does the Flipped Classroom Lead to Increased Gains on Learning Outcomes in ESL/EFL Contexts?
citation: Webb, M., & Doman, E. (2016). Does the Flipped Classroom Lead to Increased Gains on Learning Outcomes in ESL/EFL Contexts? The CATESOL Journal, 28(1). http://www.catesoljournal.org
title: Flipped ESL/EFL grammar module: out-of-class video lesson, online quiz, and discussion post per grammatical principle
description: A repeating weekly instructional pattern in which explicit grammar input moves outside class and class time is freed for application. Students "watch the video lesson, complete a follow-up online quiz, and post a sentence using the corresponding grammatical principle through an online discussion tool." In this study the pattern ran across 10 video lessons from week 3 to week 13, with quizzes graded out of 10 possible points and discussion posts pass/fail, replacing in-class mini-lectures given to control students.
requirements: Teacher-recorded video lessons plus an LMS supporting online quizzes and discussion posts
Videos kept short enough to review repeatedly; in this study an average of 10 minutes each
constraints: Grammar achievement in writing was not assessed because of course-requirement differences between contexts
Completion dipped mid-semester (weeks 6-8), so the pattern depends on monitoring student buy-in

High-intermediate EFL first-year university students in Macau
target_learning_goals: Explicit English grammar principles (sentence boundaries, verb tense and form, comma usage) assessed as student learning outcomes
examples: Flipped teachers taught none of the grammar points in class; students received identical grammar content online while control students got in-class PPT lectures and practice quizzes with no formal assessment

article_title: Flipped @ SBU: Student Satisfaction and the College Classroom
citation: Gross, B., Hoffman, M., Marinari, M., DeSimone, K., & Burke, P. (2015). Flipped @ SBU: Student satisfaction and the college classroom. Educational Research Quarterly, 39(2), 37-52.
title: Flipped instruction moves lecture content outside class and uses class time for active, learner-centered activities.
description: The flipped or inverted classroom is defined as "the practice of moving the lecture portion of the course outside of the classroom and engaging in active learning activities during class time." Course material is disseminated before class, often through short video lectures, freeing class time for collaborative problem-solving and student-centered exercises. The model assumes good teaching limits passive knowledge transfer and promotes inquiry, collaboration, and critical thinking.
requirements: Students prepare before class by engaging with disseminated materials
Instructors provide access to lecture content outside class, often via recorded videos or online resources
constraints: May increase instructor workload and preparation time
Students may be initially slow to adapt to new expectations
target_learning_goals: Active learning, collaboration, critical thinking, and student engagement
examples: Three faculty members at Saint Bonaventure University delivered courses in three disciplines using the flipped format during fall 2014.

title: Three-component unifying structure for writing curricula: fluency, content, accuracy
description: The article presents a unifying structure for writing instruction consisting of three major components that "all strategies, activities, and approaches in a well -conceived writing curriculum must promote": fluency (opportunities to practice the act of writing), content (opportunities to develop meaningful writing), and accuracy (opportunities to provide purposeful skill instruction). examples: The article lists fluency, content, and accuracy as the three components of its unifying writing curriculum structure

article_title: Engaging ESP University Students in Flipped Classrooms for Developing Functional Writing Skills, HOTs, and Eliminating Writer's Block
citation: Salem, A. A. M. S. (2018). Engaging ESP University Students in Flipped Classrooms for Developing Functional Writing Skills, HOTs, and Eliminating Writer's Block. English Language Teaching, 11(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n12p177
title: Flipped learning as a focus change from teacher-centered to learner-centered instruction
description: The article defines flipped learning not as a single procedure but as changing the focus of teaching and learning: "flipped classrooms associates with a "focus change" form teacher-centered approach into the learner-centered approach". It moves instructional content outside class (recorded lectures, online materials) and reserves in-class time for problem-solving, collaborative activities and feedback, while redefining teachers' and learners' roles and shifting learners from passive listeners to active participants. The author lists several flipping models (standard inverted, discussion-oriented, demonstration-focused, faux-flipped, group-based, virtual, flipping the teacher) and maps the flipped session's three stages onto the phases of self-regulated learning.
requirements: Instructional content must precede class as assignments, with in-class time devoted to problem-solving activities and advanced concepts
Out-of-class learning materials and resources, and teacher supervision through a learning management system, must be available
constraints: The article cautions that "flipping classrooms is not a super-hero teaching strategy" and that traditional teaching still works well with certain materials, situations and students
The author notes flipped learning has no decisive definition and no single model
target_learners: undergraduate business ESP students in higher education
examples: The study's course used pre-class recorded lectures (about 15 minutes each), one traditional campus lecture, and interactive flipped sessions where students answered exam-style questions on their own devices with immediate online formative feedback via Moodle.

article_title: The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety
citation: Nihat BAYAT. (2014). The Effect of the Process Writing Approach on Writing Success and Anxiety. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2014.3.1720
title: Flower and Hayes's cognitive process model of writing
description: The article describes the Flower and Hayes (1981) process writing approach as treating writing as a process rather than a completed product, emphasizing three dimensions: "the task environment, long-term memory, and the writing process". The writing process unit "is composed of the stages of planning, translating, and reviewing", with constant monitoring governing transitions between phases. Hayes (1996) later added a working memory unit addressing motivational and affective characteristics. The study operationalizes this model in classroom writing instruction.
requirements: Writing activities must evaluate the text as part of the writing process rather than only after completion
The teacher acts as a guide who facilitates the student's act of writing instead of presenting information
constraints: Critics cited in the article note it does not account for mental processes during text production, that ignoring grammar, structure, and the written product causes inconvenience, and that emphasis on drafts may cause students to fail exams
examples: The experimental group worked through planning, translating, and reviewing stages operationalized as brainstorming, planning, drafting, editing, and proofreading using a stage checklist

It "scrutinizes participants’ communication apprehension, test-anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation" and focuses on speaking in a classroom context. title: FLIP framework: flexible environment, learning philosophy, intentional content, professional educator
description: The article presents the flipped classroom approach as having four elements known as FLIP, attributed to the Flipped Learning Network (2014).
