citation: Adrian Leis and Kenneth Brown. (2018). Flipped learning in an EFL environment: Does the teacher's experience affect learning outcomes? The EUROCALL Review, Volume 26, No. 1. https://www.eurocall-languages.org/the-eurocall-review
title: Flipped classroom structure: content explanation moved before class, practice under teacher supervision during class, review after class
description: The article's flipped model restructures the learning cycle: before class students "watch a video explaining lesson content", during class they "do practice exercises under the teacher's supervision", and after class they review based on the teacher's advice. This contrasts with the traditional sequence in which students listen to explanations in class and practise alone afterwards. Class time must be restructured so practice occurs under the teacher's direct supervision

description: Because content explanation is delivered before class via video, class time can be devoted to practice with supervision. The authors conclude the flipped approach is "an ideal way to increase the amount of individual coaching possible in the classroom, bringing about more efficient learning", while cautioning teachers against providing so much care that students become reliant on instructors.

Teachers must remain part of the learning process rather than leaving students to self-instruct
constraints: Teachers warn that too much individual attention may make students reliant on their instructors

article_title: Analyzing the Effect of Concept Cartoon Usage on Students' Cognitive Structures Developments and Science Achievements through Flow Maps
citation: Ceylan, Ö., & Yiğit, E. A. (2018). Analyzing the Effect of Concept Cartoon Usage on Students’ Cognitive Structures Developments and Science Achievements through Flow Maps. Science Education International, 29(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Analyzing+the+Effect+of+Concept+Cartoon+Usage+through+Flow+Maps
title: Flow map technique for representing and quantifying learners' cognitive structures
description: The flow map technique elicits and quantifies a learner's cognitive structure by recording the student's sequential answers to questions and charting the statements with direct and cross links between them. As the article puts it, "With the flow map, students’ thought patterns are revealed in succession and correlated with each other by cross-links." Four parameters are calculated: size (number of ideas), richness (recurrent linkages), integratedness (richness/(size + richness)), and correctness (misconception rate). In this study flow maps were built from voice-recorded achievement-test responses before and after an 8-week unit, and used to detect misconceptions and track cognitive-structure development.
requirements: Students' verbal responses must be recorded sequentially (e.g., voice recordings of test answers) so statements and links can be charted.
Key concepts must be identified so cross-links can be established with the first sentence in which each concept occurs.
constraints: Scores did not show a normal distribution in this study, so non-parametric tests were required for analysis.
The article notes the technique reveals cognitive structures as expressed verbally; it was applied to one science unit with 7th-grade students.
target_learners: 7th-grade middle school science students (12–13 years old)
target_learning_goals: Revealing and developing students' cognitive structures about the particulate nature of matter
Detecting and addressing misconceptions in science concepts
examples: Student K21's post-test flow map: size value 8, correctness value 4, 7 cross-links, integratedness 7/(7+8) = 0.46, indicating weak academic knowledge of the unit.

citation: Mehrak Rahimi & Elham Soleymani. (2015). The Impact of Mobile Learning on Listening Anxiety and Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 8(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n10p152
title: Foreign Language Listening Anxiety Questionnaire (FLLAQ)
description: The FLLAQ (Kimura, 2008) is a 26-item self-report questionnaire assessing anxiety experienced when listening to English texts, categorized into three factors: emotional anxiety, worry, and anticipatory fear. In this study it was translated into Persian and back-translated, rated on a six-point Likert scale from 'never' to 'always', with reliability of 0.91 for the whole scale and 0.85, 0.86, and 0.80 for the subscales. It served as the pretest covariate and posttest outcome for the anxiety analysis.
requirements: Translation and back-translation to check clarity and accuracy when used in another language
examples: Used to assess participants' entry level of listening anxiety before the twelve-week intervention

description: The flipped classroom moves direct instruction outside class, usually via electronic means such as videos, and transfers application assignments into classroom time. In this study, learners watched instructor-made reading videos before class, then spent class time reflecting on, discussing, and practicing what they had learned under teacher supervision.

Inequities in students' home lives can be a barrier where students lack technology access

title: Flipped classroom model as a blended, student-centred technology-based teaching model
description: The article defines FCM as a technology-based blended learning model in which "the application of learning activities such as recollection and comprehension at home, usually online" precedes class, while higher-order practices such as application, analysis, evaluation and creation occur in the classroom. The student is active and central, with the teacher guiding rather than transmitting. The model eliminates time and space limitations, lets students revisit material at their own pace, and aims at effective use of classroom time for active learning, discussion and problem-solving.
requirements: Technological tools and internet access so students can engage with pre-class online materials
constraints: The article lists disadvantages including unequal access to computers and internet, difficulty verifying whether students watch videos, technical problems, and that lengthy or poorly prepared video lessons reduce student motivation and interest

examples: In the experimental stage, the experimental group studied theory at home via e-book and video lectures, wrote in forums, took weekly mini exams, and did high-level activities in class under instructor guidance

article_title: Measuring Engagement as Students Learn Dynamic Systems and Control with a Video Game
citation: B. D. Coller, D. J. Shernoff, and A. D. Strati. (2011). Measuring Engagement as Students Learn Dynamic Systems and Control with a Video Game. Advances in Engineering Education. https://advances.engineeringeducation.org
title: Flow Theory as the conceptual framework for student engagement
description: The article interprets engagement within the theoretical framework of Flow Theory, defining flow as a state of deep absorption in an activity that is intrinsically enjoyable. Based on flow theory, student engagement was conceptualized as the simultaneous occurrence of high concentration, enjoyment, and interest. This conceptualization is meant to capture experiences combining the focused, disciplined aspects of work with enjoyable aspects of leisure. The study used this framework to structure its Experience Sampling Method measures and its composite engagement variables.
requirements: Engagement is measured as the simultaneous occurrence of high concentration, enjoyment, and interest, consistent with the flow-theory conceptualization.
constraints: Flow occurs when individuals stretch the limits of their abilities to meet challenges, such that skills are neither overmatched nor underutilized.
examples: The perception of the activity as like Work and Play was the category that best represents flow in the study's analyses.

citation: Boudadi, N. A., & Gutiérrez-Colón, M. (2020). Effect of Gamification on students' motivation and learning achievement in Second Language Acquisition within higher education: a literature review 2011-2019. The EUROCALL Review, 28(1). http://eurocall.webs.upv.es/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Azzouz_Literature_review_tables.pdf
title: Flow theory and the engagement loop: sustained motivation from challenge-skill balance
description: The review presents Flow theory as an account of sustained motivation arising from a balanced relation between challenge and a person's sense of efficacy based on their skills. Citing Csikszentmihalyi (1991), the authors note "people reach the Flow state when they stick to an activity for the sake only of its enjoyment and gratification". This connects to Zichermann and Cunningham's 'engagement loop', in which players constantly seek satisfaction through regular rewards, and to Bandura's self-efficacy construct, where positive outcomes such as self-fulfilment boost and sustain intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Gamified activities should follow a progressive system with sequenced levels through which players can advance at their own pace
constraints: The review notes little evidence supporting positive effects on cognitive processes and calls for research on long-term effects
target_learners: higher education students learning a second language
target_learning_goals: sustained motivation and engagement in learning tasks
examples: Hamari et al. (2016) explored correlations between Flow variables (challenge and skills), engagement, immersion and perceived learning in engineering education with positive results

title: Theoretical foundations of flipped learning: constructivism, Bloom's revised taxonomy, and Kolb's experiential cycle
description: The article grounds flipped learning in three established theories. Constructivist learning theory holds that students learn best when actively constructing knowledge through experience and reflection, underpinning FL's pre-class preparation and in-class participation. The article states that "the model aligns with Bloom's revised taxonomy, which encourages shifting lower-order cognitive activities (e.g., remembering, understanding) to pre-class tasks, while using class time for higher-order skills like applying, analyzing, and evaluating." FL is also presented as supporting Kolb's experiential learning cycle of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation.
requirements: Pre-class materials and tasks must be provided so lower-order activities can be shifted out of class time
constraints: The article presents these as the pedagogical foundation of FL rather than testing them empirically in this study

examples: The study's course design embedded pre-class preparation, in-class application through discussions and case studies, and post-class reflection

description: This element is the article's teaching model: students watch an expert demonstration video before class, then practice in self-directed triads where "each of the triads consisted of a “performer”, a “coach” and a “monitor"" — the performer practices hands-on, the coach gives just-in-time feedback, and the monitor assesses performance and feedback quality. Roles rotate through three 10-minute segments, tutors answer questions but give no hands-on demonstrations, and laminated handouts, videos and rubrics are available for reference. It was trialed with 205 penultimate-year medical students learning bag mask ventilation and intravenous cannulation.
requirements: Students must be assigned and rotate through the performer, coach and monitor roles, with demonstration videos and assessment rubrics available for reference during practice
constraints: The article notes students were not immediately corrected after observing a flawed performance, and tutors reported some monitors gave feedback when not supposed to, so student compliance impacts execution
target_learning_goals: clinical procedural skills such as bag mask ventilation and intravenous cannulation
examples: 205 fifth-year medical students learned BMV and IVC in 3-hour sessions of 10–12 students, each practicing in a triad at least once with roles rotating every 10 minutes

article_title: An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case-based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education.
citation: Lundegren N, Jönsson A, Lindberg P. (2021). An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case‐based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education. European Journal of Dental Education, 25(4), 649-656. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12642
title: Flipped classroom seminar structure: individual quiz, small-group agreement and vote, then lecturer-led discussion
description: This lesson-level pattern sequences a teaching block as lecture with reading instructions or a case, individual and group preparation, then a flipped classroom seminar. As the article describes it, "The seminar starts with an individual quiz (circa 7 items with 4 alternatives), and then, the items from the quiz are discussed, one at a time, in small groups (5–7 students), where the group must come to an agreement and vote on which alternative they find the most correct." The lecturer then leads discussion in which each group justifies its choice, and students analyse, synthesise and evaluate course content to construct shared meaning. Seminars are mandatory; absent students receive a written assignment reviewed by a peer.
requirements: Students prepare individually before the seminar
A lecturer leads the seminar while students contribute most to the discussions
constraints: During the COVID-19 pandemic the seminars were run virtually in Zoom using chat and break-out rooms, mimicking real-life seminar design
target_learning_goals: analysing, synthesising and evaluating course content
examples: Figure 2 describes the seminar flow; Figure 3 shows a periodontology quiz item on the pseudo-pocket used in semester two

title: Flipped active-learning sections structured around preclass work, daily quizzes, and group in-class activities
description: The flipped sections used a highly standardized three-component weekly structure. Students completed interactive SoftChalk modules and online homework before class worth 10% of the grade, took individual-then-group reading quizzes at the start of class, and spent the remaining class time in group activities such as "worksheets with practice problems and case studies, model building, card sorts, games, group discussions, and acting out concepts," done in groups of two to four while instructors circulated. The in-class activities were not worth points toward grades.
requirements: Students complete an interactive-learning module and an online homework assignment before attending each class
A single instructor per section with highly standardized shared materials across flipped sections
constraints: The in-class activities were not worth points toward student grades
target_learners: Community college students in a first-semester majors' general biology course
target_learning_goals: Mastery of general biology concepts and transferable study skills for subsequent science courses
examples: Students sat at tables in groups of four, were randomly regrouped weekly, answered five quiz questions individually then five as a group, and built their own representations of concepts by drawing, describing, or constructing models

article_title: Flipped learning enhances non-technical skill performance in simulation-based education: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Moll-Khosrawi Parisa, Zöllner Christian, Cencin Nadine, Schulte-Uentrop Leonie. (2021). Flipped learning enhances non-technical skill performance in simulation-based education: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02766-w
title: Flipped learning as an instructional approach inverting classroom-based learning
description: The article describes flipped learning as an instructional approach in which "the traditional concept and idea of classroom-based learning is inverted": new content is first mastered through structured activities in the individual learning space, and face-to-face group time is used for active learning strategies and concept application. In this trial the approach was operationalised via the four pillars of F-L-I-P (flexible environment, learning culture, intentional content, professional educator), a brief seminar, individual learning assignments including a written debriefing, and student-conducted debriefings in the second training.
requirements: Proper planning and organisation with adequate learning guidance for the individual learning phase; the article states flipping a class by merely having learners read additional material does not necessarily result in flipped learning
constraints: The article notes the theoretical teaching approach designed for the individual learning space might, according to constructive alignment, be objected to as inappropriate, an objection the authors overrule
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills (planning and problem-solving, teamwork and leadership, team orientation) in emergency simulation training
examples: Students prepared on NTS and the AS-NTS rating system in the individual learning space, completed a written cold debriefing of baseline scenarios, then conducted peer debriefings with AS-NTS scores in the second training while instructors acted as facilitators
key_sources: Moll-Khosrawi Parisa, Zöllner Christian, Cencin Nadine, Schulte-Uentrop Leonie. (2021). Flipped learning enhances non-technical skill performance in simulation-based education: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02766-w

citation: Moll-Khosrawi Parisa, Zöllner Christian, Cencin Nadine, Schulte-Uentrop Leonie. (2021). Flipped learning enhances non-technical skill performance in simulation-based education: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02766-w
title: Combine flipped learning with simulation-based medical education to teach non-technical skills
description: The article recommends applying a flipped learning approach in combination with SBME to complement the learning process of non-technical skills, because the individual learning space lets students control their learning speed, reflect on behavioural benchmarks, and build mental models before applying them in simulation. The authors state their "suggested approach is easy assessable, easy to implement and cost-effective" and that the brief seminar can be replaced with a video on online platforms.
requirements: Structured individual learning assignments with provided teaching materials and clear tasks; preparation responsibility such as preparing to conduct debriefings; proper planning and organisation of the flipped design
constraints: The article prints no information on which component of the flipped learning had the greatest effect; the intervention might have been too short to affect motivation; medical educators were not blinded
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in simulation-based emergency training
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills such as planning and problem-solving, teamwork and leadership, and team orientation
examples: In the trial, students received a brief NTS seminar, worked through provided materials, completed a written cold debriefing of baseline scenarios, and then conducted peer debriefings with AS-NTS scores during the second simulation training

title: Flexible e-learning video approach for fundus examination skills
description: A 10-minute e-learning video demonstrating fundus examination skills, streamed so students can "watch the video repeatedly on their smartphone, tablet, or PC" before skills practice. In the study it replaced a 10-minute face-to-face lecture of identical content and images, and was paired with simulator practice and iExaminer-based training sessions. The authors position it as filling a gap in procedural skill training where traditional lecture-based teaching yields low clinician confidence.
requirements: Access to a video streaming server and personal devices (smartphone, tablet, or PC) for flexible viewing
Contract or safeguard to prevent sharing the video with students who have not yet completed the assessment
A paired hands-on training component (in the study, 30-minute ophthalmoscope training sessions)
constraints: Effects were demonstrated on a simulator, not with real patients
Results may not generalize beyond the sampled population; validation needed for residents and general physicians
Video viewing frequency and duration were not measured
target_learners: fifth-year medical students in general medicine clerkship
target_learning_goals: confidence and motivation to perform ophthalmoscopy
examples: Students in the intervention groups watched the video via a streaming server 48 hours before the questionnaire and pre-test simulation, then completed 30-minute standardized ophthalmoscope training sessions

citation: Kim Sin-Hyang, Park Sihyun. (2021). Influence of learning flow and distance e-learning satisfaction on learning outcomes and the moderated mediation effect of social-evaluative anxiety in nursing college students during the COVID-19 pandemic: A cross-sectional study. Nurse Education in Practice. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nepr.2021.103197
title: Hypothesis conceptual model: learning flow affects learning outcomes via distance e-learning satisfaction, moderated by social-evaluative anxiety
description: The article proposes and tests a conditional process model in which learning flow — "a state where the entire mind is fully concentrated on a particular activity" — influences learning outcomes indirectly through distance e-learning satisfaction, with COVID-19-related social-evaluative anxiety moderating the first-stage path. Social-evaluative anxiety is operationally defined as experiences of fear, distress, anxiety, or discomfort related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The model was tested with PROCESS Macro Models 4 and 7 and, in the authors' words, "our hypothesis conceptual model was statistically confirmed".
requirements: Measurement of learning flow, distance e-learning satisfaction, learning outcomes, and social-evaluative anxiety with validated scales
constraints: Tested only in a cross-sectional design with nursing students in South Korea during the COVID-19 pandemic; causality cannot be inferred per the article's limitations
examples: Fig. 2 illustrates the final model with path coefficients, including the learning flow × SEA interaction on DE-LS (B = −0.59)

article_title: Utilizing transcranial direct current stimulation to enhance laparoscopic technical skills training: A randomized controlled trial.
citation: Cox Morgan L., Deng Zhi-De, Palmer Hannah, Watts Amanda, Beynel Lysianne, Young Jonathan R., Lisanby Sarah H., Migaly John, Appelbaum Lawrence G. (2020). Utilizing transcranial direct current stimulation to enhance laparoscopic technical skills training: A randomized controlled trial. Brain Stimulation. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brs.2020.03.009
title: FLS Peg Transfer training protocol with error-penalized overall score
description: The study's training element is the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery Task 1 Peg Transfer performed in a box trainer across six 20-min blocks over three visits, preceded and followed by single timed pre- and post-tests. Performance was scored by an overall score in which "Total Error Deduction = 3 × drops outside the field-of-view + 1 × improper transfers", subtracted from total objects moved. Training blocks were paired with active or sham tDCS delivered concurrently with practice.
requirements: An FLS box trainer, the standard instructional video, and timed single-trial pre- and post-tests; stimulation delivered concurrently with 20-min practice blocks
constraints: Errors were penalized 3 points for drops outside the field of view and 1 point for improper transfers, per the article's scoring formula
target_learners: Healthy adult novices without prior laparoscopic experience (mean age 22.7, 42 females)
target_learning_goals: Bimanual laparoscopic technical skill acquisition on the FLS Peg Transfer task
examples: Sixty subjects completed six 20-min training blocks across three visits, with overall scores rising from e.g. bM1 123.4 to 220.1 across blocks

title: Flow State Scale (FSS) as a self-report measure of practitioner involvement in simulation training
description: The Flow State Scale is a self-report test used in this study to gauge realism, involvement and stress management during simulation. The article describes it as follows: "The FSS consists of 36 items divided into 9 subscales, the short flow scale (SFSS), each representing the nine different dimensions of Flow", scored 1–5 (never to always) and administered after each scenario session. The nine dimensions include challenge-skill balance, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time transformation and autotelic experience.
requirements: Administered to participants after each scenario session
All 36 items answered by participants
constraints: The authors state data evaluating FSS changes during team training in HFS was still lacking prior to this study
target_learning_goals: Measuring flow, involvement and stress management during team training
examples: FSS was administered at the end of the Model 1 and Model 2 scenarios to the same 43 practitioners, and item and subscale medians were compared between courses

constraints: Applied here to a primary-school natural sciences/nutrition unit; the article notes gamification is distinct from an educational game

examples: The day before class the teacher uploaded a video students watched and completed a viewing questionnaire; class sessions carried out practical activities
